papers.version_note: The text layer holds the paper twice (page-order copy, then a column-order copy). The first copy was read in full; the second was used only to check quotes and table rows.
papers.what_it_is: A paper that casts SVM training as a QUBO problem, trains it on a D-Wave Advantage annealer, and compares accuracy and training time with Scikit-learn and simulated annealing.

existing.note: The abstract says accuracies are on par. The Discussion limits this: the quantum approach is better on one dataset, equal on some, and outperformed on five, and the authors say only that it is in the same ballpark for most datasets.
existing.value: The authors report from Table 1 that the quantum approach performs better than the classical approach in case of Wine 1–2, equals it on some datasets such as synthetic and Iris, and is outperformed by the classical approach on Iris Versicolor-Virginica, WBC, Wine 0–2, Digits, and Lambeq; they state that within the constraints of the quantum architecture the accuracies were in the same ballpark as the classical approach for most of the datasets.
quotes: The testing accuracies presented in Table 1 show that the quantum approach performs better than the classical approach in case of Wine 1–2.
On some datasets such as synthetic and Iris, it equals the performance of the classical approach.
On other datasets however (Iris VersicolorVirginica, WBC, Wine 0–2, Digits, and Lambeq), it is outperformed by the classical approach.
Within the constraints imposed by the quantum architecture, the quantum approach was able to produce accuracies that were in the same ballpark as the classical approach for most of the datasets.
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study on small training sets.
existing.reader_inference: The headline 'on par' statement hides that the quantum model was worse on five of the nine dataset groups, and much worse on Iris Versicolor-Virginica.

existing.note: The paper adds one exception to the no-difference statement: the Iris Versicolor-Virginica pair had less variance and higher accuracy at the longest annealing time.
existing.value: The authors report that as the annealing time increased, the Scikit-learn model consistently performed better and had less variance in accuracy than the quantum and simulated annealing models, and that increasing the annealing time gave no statistically significant difference in accuracy because the mean accuracies of each test were within one standard deviation of each other; however, they state that the Iris data set with the classes Virginica and Versicolor saw less variance and higher training and testing accuracy when trained for 1, 000μs as compared to 20μs.
quotes: Even as the annealing time increased, the Scikit-learn model consistently performed better and consisted less variance in accuracy than the quantum and simulated annealing models.
There wasn't a statistically significant difference in the accuracy by increasing the annealing time as the mean accuracies of each test were within one standard deviation of each other.
However, the Iris data set with the classes Virginica and Versicolor saw less variance and higher training and testing accuracy when trained for 1, 000μs as compared to 20μs.
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, ten repetitions per condition.

existing.note: The conclusion's 4.48 times figure is the 52-point result of the data-point study at 8 million features. The feature study at 52 points and 8 million features reports 3.69 times. The speedup holds only for large feature counts: the classical approach was faster for up to 1,048,576 features, and the speedup fell to 1.72 times at 54 points.
existing.value: The authors report a speedup of 3.69× over the classical approach when training with up to 8 million features, and a speedup by a factor of 4.48 at 52 points in the data-point study; at 54 points the quantum SVM is 1.72× faster; with a smaller number of features (d ≤ 1,048,576) the classical approach's runtime is faster than the D-Wave approach. They note that the Scikit-learn algorithm may not be the most efficient classical algorithm.
quotes: When training with up to 8 million features, the quantum approach exhibits a speedup of 3.69× over the classical approach.
At 52 points, where the quantum computer could find an embedding with minimal time fluctuation, the quantum computer outperforms the classical computer by a factor of 4.48.
However, even at 54 points, the quantum SVM is 1.72× faster than its classical counterpart.
With smaller number of features (d ≤ 1,048,576), the classical approach's runtime is faster than the D-Wave approach.
While the Scikit-learn's algorithm for training SVMs may not be the most efficient classical algorithm
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical timing result from one study against one classical solver.
existing.reader_inference: Table 3 and Table 4 rows give the same ratios: 6,920.407 ms against 1,877.741 ms is 3.69; 7,194.556 ms against 1,606.784 ms is 4.48. The baseline is Scikit-learn on 52 training points, so the comparison is at a tiny N.

existing.note: The paper's general result keeps K, the number of binary variables per multiplier: qubit footprint and time are both of order N squared times K squared. The quadratic figure holds only if K is a fixed constant, and the analysis assumes a constant annealing time and constant repetitions for problems that fit the annealer.
existing.value: The paper states that the qubit footprint and time complexity of the quantum approach are both of order N squared times K squared when K is a variable, and that if the precision for all parameters is fixed so that K is a constant factor, both become of order N squared, which it calls an order of magnitude better than the classical algorithm, of order N cubed. The authors assume that a constant annealing time and a constant number of repetitions seem to work well in practice, and state that estimating ST99 and ST99(OPT) for generic QUBO formulation of the SVM problem is beyond the scope of the present work.
quotes: Note that the qubit footprint O(N 2K2) and time complexity O(N 2K2) assume that K is a variable.
The resulting qubit footprint would be O(N 2), and time complexity would also be be O(N 2). This time complexity is an order of magnitude better than the classical algorithm (O(N 3)).
For problems within this range, a constant annealing time and a constant number of repetitions seem to work well in practice.
Estimating ST99 and ST99(OPT) for generic QUBO formulation of the SVM problem is beyond the scope of the present work.
existing.certainty_reason: An analytic complexity under stated assumptions; no formal theorem or proof is given.
existing.reader_inference: The text says 'linear regression problem' where the SVM is meant, in the sentence that gives the total time; this looks like text carried over from the authors' linear regression paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that they convert the SVM training problem, through its Lagrangian dual and a binary encoding of the multipliers, into a QUBO problem (their Equation 13) with M = KN, which can then be solved on adiabatic quantum computers.
quotes: Equation 13 is identical to Eq. 6 with z = λˆ, A = 1 2 P T (X X T ⊙ Y Y T )P, b = −PT 1N , and M = KN.
Hence, we converted the SVM training problem from Eq. 2 into a QUBO problem in Eq. 13, which can then be solved on AQCs.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4 defines the formulation step by step (Equations 6 to 13).

assertions.value: The authors define a K-dimensional precision vector whose entries are each a power of 2, and introduce K binary variables for each Lagrangian multiplier, so that each multiplier is a weighted sum of binary variables; they state that this is required to impose the non-negativity constraint.
quotes: We now introduce a K-dimensional precision vector, P = [p1, p2, . . . , pK ]T , where each entry pk is a power of 2.
This is required to impose the non-negativity constraint on λ.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4 defines the precision vector and the binary encoding.
assertions.reader_inference: The number of bits K per multiplier sets the numerical precision of the learned weights; the Discussion ties accuracy losses to this.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QUBO formulation has a number of variables of order K times N, and that the qubit footprint (space complexity) of the formulation is of order N squared times K squared after embedding onto the hardware.
quotes: So, the total number of variables in Eq. 13 is O(KN ). So, the qubit footprint (or space complexity) of this formulation would be O(N 2K2) after embedding onto the hardware.
assertions.certainty_reason: An analytic space bound stated without a derivation of the embedding overhead beyond a citation.

assertions.value: The authors state that the time to convert the SVM problem into a QUBO problem is of order N squared times K squared, inferred from Equations 7 and 9, and that embedding can be done in the same order of time using the embedding algorithm of Date and co-authors.
quotes: converting Problem 1 into a QUBO problem can be inferred from Eqs. 7 and 9 as O(N 2K2). Because we have O(N K) variables in the QUBO formulation, embedding can be done in O(N 2K2) time
assertions.certainty_reason: An analytic complexity; the embedding time rests on a cited algorithm.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Bottou and Lin, that the time complexity of classical SVM algorithms is of order N cubed, and that the Lagrangian dual problem is solved in order N cubed time on classical computers.
quotes: The time complexity of classical SVM algorithms is O(N 3) (Bottou & Lin, 2007).
The Lagrangian dual problem (Eq. 2) is solved in O(N 3) time on classical computers
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.
assertions.reader_inference: The measured Scikit-learn solver is SMO-based, and the paper itself says it may not be the most efficient classical algorithm.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Mukherjee and Chakrabarti, that the theoretical time complexity of quantum annealing used to obtain an exact solution is exponential, and that a more realistic estimate of the running time uses measures such as ST99 and ST99(OPT), which give the expected number of iterations to reach a certain level of optimality with 99% certainty.
quotes: used to obtain an exact solution is exponential

a more realistic estimate of the running time can be made by using measures such as ST99 and ST99(OPT) (Wang & Jonckheere, 2019), which give the expected number of iterations to reach a certain level of optimality with 99% certainty.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not estimate these measures for its own problem (see the quoted scope statement in the time-complexity entry), so its quadratic claim rests on a constant-annealing-time assumption.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing earlier work, that a D-Wave 2000Q can accommodate problems with 64 or fewer binary variables that require all-to-all connectivity.
quotes: DWave 2000Q can accommodate problems with 64 or fewer binary variables that require all-to-all connectivity (Date et al., 2019a).
assertions.certainty_reason: A hardware fact the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors used the D-Wave Advantage quantum annealer, which offers 5,627 functioning qubits, embedded problems with the EmbeddingComposite class, ran 10 annealing runs for each problem instance, and selected the solution with the lowest energy sample.
quotes: We used the D-Wave Advantage quantum annealer to evaluate the quantum approach; the annealer offers 5,627 functioning qubits.
We conducted 10 annealing runs for each problem instance to ensure accuracy and selected the solution with the lowest energy sample.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own hardware and run setup (Section 5.2).

assertions.value: The authors ran the classical approach, simulated annealing and preprocessing on two machines: an AMD Ryzen 4600H 6-core CPU at 3 GHz with 16 GB of RAM for the accuracy results, and an Intel Xeon E5-2690v4 14-core CPU at 2.6 GHz with 64 GB of RAM for the compute-time results.
quotes: The first system, equipped with an AMD Ryzen 4600H 6-core CPU running at 3 GHz and 16 GB of DDR4 RAM running at 2,666 MHz, was used to evaluate the accuracy results described in Section 5.4.
The second system, equipped with an Intel Xeon E5-2690v4 14-core CPU running at 2.6 GHz and 64 GB of DDR4 RAM running at 2,400 MHz, was used to evaluate the compute times presented in Section 5.6.

assertions.reader_inference: The Conclusion names the first CPU as AMD Ryzen 5 4600H; this is the same part.

assertions.value: The authors measure the classical compute time as the time taken for training, and the quantum compute time as the time to convert the problem into a QUBO problem, embed it onto the quantum hardware, and perform quantum annealing; the network overhead time to the D-Wave server is not considered in the total computation time.
quotes: For the classical approach, we measure the compute time as the time taken for training.

the compute time for the quantum approach encompasses the time required for converting the problem into a QUBO problem, embedding the QUBO problem onto the quantum hardware, and performing quantum annealing to solve the problem.
Although not considered for the total computation time, the network overhead time increases as the number of points increases.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 5.1 defines the compute-time metric used for every timing result.
assertions.reader_inference: Table 3 and Table 4 show network overhead in the hundreds of thousands of milliseconds at 52 points, far above the compute times, and it is excluded from the speedup.

assertions.value: The authors compare Scikit-learn, which solves SVMs with the sequential minimal optimization algorithm, with the quantum SVM and simulated annealing; they run 10 rounds of training and testing per dataset and, for many datasets, train on only 52 points chosen uniformly at random because 52 is the largest training set that could be accommodated on the annealer.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum computing applications in High Energy Physics: clustering, integration and generative models (PhD thesis, arXiv:2512.01597v1)
papers.version_note: The text layer holds the thesis twice: a page-order copy of the whole document (185 numbered pages plus front matter), then a layout copy that starts again at the title page. The first copy was read in full, from the title page to the last reference, including the Spanish summary (Chapter 8), the three appendices and the bibliography; the second copy was used only to check quotes. Exponents are printed flat in the text layer (for example O(N 3) for N cubed, 103 for ten to the third).
papers.what_it_is: A doctoral thesis that applies quantum algorithms to three high-energy-physics problems: quantum jet clustering with a Minkowski-distance SwapTest and a quantum maximum search (Chapter 4), the QFIAE quantum Monte Carlo integrator applied to loop Feynman integrals and NLO decay rates (Chapter 5), and quantum Chebyshev probabilistic models for fragmentation functions (Chapter 6).

assertions.value: The authors state that the Quantum Marginal Problem is an important and mostly open problem, that for general graphs it has so far been solved only for disjoint subsystems, and that for trees it is possible to reconstruct a quantum state from its two-body marginals; they say that studying the defining equations of the varieties might open a new way of attacking the problem.

papers.what_it_is: A theory paper that extends the agent-environment framework of learning to quantum systems with a tester, proves that classical and classically tested interactions give no quantum gain beyond computational complexity, and gives a Grover-based construction of a quantum reinforcement learning agent that beats a luck-favoring classical agent in deterministic, strictly epochal, single-win environments.

existing.note: The conclusion states the quadratic gain generally. The body limits it: it holds for restricted task environments, rests on luck-favoring pairs and on untested oracular access, and the authors say making the quadratic claim formal needs a specified learning model. The exponential figure is a ratio of performances at one time scale, for an epsilon-greedy agent.
existing.value: The paper states that its constructed quantum reinforcement learning agents outperform their classical counterparts quadratically in terms of learning efficiency, or even exponentially in performance over limited periods; the body qualifies this: the results are obtained at the cost of restricting the task environments, the exponential ratio is for an agent using a variant of epsilon-greedy behavior and holds for time-scales T ∈ O(t), and making the quadratic claim more formal requires further specifying the underlying learning model.

assertions.value: The authors set learning in the paradigm of learning agents: an agent A interacts with an unknown environment E through messages, actions issued by A and percepts issued by E; in the quantum extension these sets become Hilbert spaces, and the agent and environment are described as sequences of completely positive trace-preserving maps acting on a common communication register.

quotes: Here we consider a learning agent A (equivalently a learning program A) which interacts with an unknown environment E (the so-called task environment, or problem setting) via the exchange of messages
In the quantum extension, these sets become Hilbert spaces, HA = span{|ai }, HS = span{|si }, and form orthonormal bases.
The agent (environment) is specified by sequences of completely positive trace preserving (CPTP) maps
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its framework in the main text and in Appendix I.

assertions.value: The authors state that in reinforcement learning sample complexity is usually substituted by learning efficiency, the number of interaction steps needed for the agent to learn to obtain the rewards with high probability, and that recent results in quantum machine learning have focused on improving computational complexity, with only few recent works considering sample complexity aspects.
quotes: In RL, sample complexity is usually substituted by learning efficiency – the number of interaction steps needed for the agent to learn to obtain the rewards with high probability.

The recent results in QML have focused on improving computational complexity [5–8, 10], with only few recent works considering sample complexity aspects [11] or supervised computational learning [12, 13].
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the efficiency measure it improves; the literature remark is an author statement.

assertions.value: The authors define a tester as a third entity, a sequence of controlled maps acting on an external register and the communication register, applied after each map of the agent and the environment; a classical tester copies all the states of the communication register to its own, and the quantum history is the state of the tester register.
quotes: We formalize and and characterize a quantum history more broadly by introducing a third entity - a tester.
In the tested interaction between an agent and the environment, the map of the tester is applied after each map of both the agent and the environment.
A classical tester copies all the states of the RC register to its own.
assertions.certainty_reason: Appendix I defines the tester.

assertions.value: The authors define an agent as classical if its maps neither generate entanglement, nor coherent superpositions of classical states, when acting on classical states (Definition 1), and define a classical interaction as one where at every stage the state of the combined registers is a mixture of products with the interface register a convex mixture of classical states (Definition 2); they note that a classical interaction does not require the agent and environment to be internally in classical states.

In other words, the agent A is classical if its maps neither generate entanglement, nor coherent superpositions of classical states, when acting on classical states.

Definition 2. The interaction between the agent A and the environment E is called a classical interaction if at every stage of the interaction, the state of the combined registers can be represented in the form
Given Definition 2, a classical interaction between an agent and the environment does not entail that the agent and the environment are internally in classical states.

assertions.value: The paper proves (Lemma 1) that for any agent A and environment E, A and E have a classical interaction if and only if the reduced state of the three registers RA, RC and RE is the same in the presence and absence of a classical tester, by a direct argument for one direction and an induction over interaction steps for the other.
quotes: Lemma 1. For any agent A and environment E, A and E have a classical interaction if and only if the (reduced) state of the three registers of RARC RE is the same in the presence and absence of a classical tester.
We prove this direction by induction over interaction steps.
assertions.certainty_reason: Lemma 1 is stated for any agent and environment and proved in Appendix I.

assertions.value: The paper proves (Lemma 2) that for any agent A and environment E which have a classical interaction when untested, there exist a classical agent Ac and a classical environment Ec generating the same quantum history for any tester and any history length, by storing classical descriptions of the quantum states, which may imply an exponential blow up in the number of registers and computation time.
quotes: Lemma 2. For any agent A and environment E, which have classical interaction (when untested), there exists a classical agent Ac and a classical environment Ec, such that ρtT (A, E) = ρtT (Ac, Ec), for any tester T, and any history length t.
This may imply an exponential blow up in the number of registers needed, (and in the computation time), but this is irrelevant in the synchronous model of agent-environment interaction.
assertions.certainty_reason: Lemma 2 is stated with its condition (classical interaction) and proved by classical simulation of the stored states.
assertions.reader_inference: The simulation cost can be exponential, so the lemma removes any gain in learning efficiency, not necessarily in computational cost; the paper states this separately in the main text.

assertions.value: The paper proves (Lemma 3) that for any agent A and environment E over compatible percept and action spaces there exist a classical agent Ac and a classical environment Ec such that the quantum history relative to the classical tester is the same for any history length, so quantum improvements are not possible in the presence of a classical tester; the authors state that the same argument cannot be used for other testers.
quotes: Lemma 3. Let A and E be any agent and any environment over compatible percept/action spaces. Then there exists a classical agent Ac and a classical environment Ec, such that ρtTc (A, E) = ρtTc (Ac, Ec), for the classical tester Tc, and any history length t.
Note that we cannot use the same argument for other testers
assertions.certainty_reason: Lemma 3 is stated for any agent and environment under the classical tester and proved in Appendix I using Lemma 2.
assertions.reader_inference: This is why the paper's quantum gain needs a sporadic tester that leaves a period of interaction untested.

assertions.value: The paper proves (Lemma 4) that for the classical equivalence class of an environment E there exists a quantum environment Eq in the class which prohibits any quantum improvement, because any quantum history relative to any tester can be realized with a fully classical agent and this environment; the authors say this asserts that the answer may be a trivial no unless further assumptions are made on how the environment extends to a full quantum system.
quotes: Lemma 4. Let Ec(E) be the classical equivalence class for some environment E. Then there exits a quantum environment Eq ∈ Ec(E) which prohibits any quantum improvement
that is, any possible quantum history (relative to any tester) can be realized with a fully classical agent and this environment Eq.
Lemma 4 then asserts that the answer may be a trivial no, unless further assumptions are made on how the environment extends to a full quantum system.
assertions.certainty_reason: Lemma 4 is stated and proved in Appendix I by inserting classical basis measurements into each map of the environment.
assertions.reader_inference: The result is a limit on the whole program: a classically specified environment guarantees no quantum gain, so any gain needs extra assumptions about the quantum extension, as the oracle constructions make.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the QC and classically tested settings the improvements are bound to computational complexity, that improvements in learning efficiency require a special type of access to the environments which is not fully tested, and that in more general settings the environment stores the actions of the agent in its memory, which effectively breaks the entanglement in the agent's register and prohibits all interference effects, although for many settings it is still possible to dissect the maps of the environment and provide oracular variants.
assertions.anchor: Section Scope and limits of quantum improvements, p.3
quotes: In the QC and classically tested settings, we are bound to computational complexity improvements, which have been achieved in certain cases.
Improvements in learning efficiency require special type of access to the environments, which is not fully tested.
This effectively breaks the entanglement in the agent's register RA, and prohibits all interference effects.
Nonetheless, for many environmental settings, it is still possible to 'dissect' the maps of the environment, and to provide oracular variants, which we can use to help the agent learn.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the scope and limits of its approach in the Scope section.

assertions.value: The authors propose a schema with three steps: define fair unitary oracular equivalents Eq of a classical environment E that should not provide more information than E under classical access, identify particular environmental properties that can be more efficiently ascertained using Eq and are relevant for learning, and construct an improved agent which uses these properties.
assertions.anchor: Section An approach to quantum improvements in reinforcement learning, p.3
quotes: First, given a classical environment E, we define fair unitary oracular equivalents Eq.
Eq should not provide more information than E under classical access, which is guaranteed, e.g., when Eq is realizable from a reversible version of E.
we identify particular environmental properties which can be more efficiently ascertained using Eq, and which are relevant for learning.
Third, we construct an improved agent which uses the properties from the previous points.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its schema in this section.

assertions.value: The authors state that for deterministic, simple strictly epochal environments, in which the environment is re-set after M steps and at most one reward is given, the construction of an appropriate oracle is dramatically simplified, giving a phase-flip oracle, and that one use of this environment-specific oracle requires M interaction steps.

assertions.reader_inference: The oracle is phase kick-back on a reversible, self-inverse implementation of the environment, so the environment must be reversible and returns no percepts.
